name: Yusuf Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and supervise tax returns for small manufacturers at Harborline Accounts. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm one of the strongest there at reconciling stock records to the tax figures. I like the moment a factory owner finally understands why cash and profit differ; I don't like receiving a crate of invoices on filing day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your pay, home and savings like, and where does AI fit today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Anika and I have no children yet; she runs the front desk at a dental clinic. I earn more than most accountants in this role, have ten months of expenses saved, and could reach plenty of other accounting firms by train. I use AI now and then to draft a note after colleagues have tested the tool, but I always check the stock figures myself. I believe a business should pay for the skill it needs, and families should first help their own when trouble comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little automation of invoice sorting is fine if the partners can show where a figure came from. The owner still needs a person who knows the business to sign off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage looks safe, and ten months saved means a short quiet patch would not shake our home. Anika and I are hoping to save for a child, so I do not want a software subscription eating the pay rise without proof it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the manufacturer returns and ask for a simple cost report before the firm buys another sorting tool. In the first year I'd put two hundred a month into our family savings pot, just as we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my job. The family plan is real, but our wages and savings give us room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cost report show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The subscription fee, the hours saved and the errors somebody had to fix. A cheap program is expensive if it sends the wrong stock value to a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after one of the team has shown a good test on old files. I can learn a proven tool, but I won't feed a live return into a novelty.

say: I would accept **invoice sorting** after the firm shows its cost and errors.
I would keep a **human signer** who understands each manufacturer.
think: My **wage feels safe** with ten months of expenses saved.
An unproven **subscription** could consume money meant for a child.
do: Keep leading **manufacturer tax returns** with current stock checks and a named human review.
Save **two hundred monthly** in our family pot.
feel: He feels **calm** about income and his family savings plan.
S0.quote: A cheap program is expensive if it sends the wrong stock value to a client.
fieldNote: He relates the tool’s value to **stock errors** and subscription cost, not to novelty.
The family savings target predates AI and sits on **strong pay** and ten months saved.

steps.text: Keep leading Harborline manufacturer tax returns with current checks
Save two hundred monthly in family savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to train the people who already know the factories before hiring a system to do their paperwork. A paid trial is sensible if we can count the wrong answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can do much of my checking and client writing, so the firm may need fewer return hours even if I remain lead. There are plenty of local firms, but they may all be hiring fewer accountants at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid two-week trial on ten finished manufacturer returns, with the staff member who knows each client checking the output. In the first year of steady change I'd take a short vendor lesson on the firm's time if the trial cuts errors, and I'd keep saving two hundred monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the hours, though I do not yet expect to lose my own salary. I want evidence before changing the review desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer corrected stock figures than our current method, with no extra unpaid evening work. If AI stock-review software simply moves mistakes to the reviewer, I would tell the partners the saving is false.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior who sorts invoices could have less to do. I would teach that junior how a factory's stock ledger links to its tax return, provided the firm gives us paid time.

say: I would run a **paid trial** on completed factory files.
I would teach a junior **stock ledgers** on paid time.
think: My **checking hours** could shrink, even if I keep the lead role.
Local firms may all **hire less** at once.
do: Run a **paid ten-return trial**; take the vendor lesson on firm time only if errors fall.
Teach the **junior stock ledgers** only if the firm gives us paid time.
Keep adding **two hundred monthly** to family savings from wages.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about hours but expects his salary to hold for now.
S1.quote: If AI stock-review software simply moves mistakes to the reviewer, I would tell the partners the saving is false.
fieldNote: He accepts tools through a **measured paid trial**, fitting his habit of waiting for proof.
His concern for the junior leads to **paid ledger teaching**, while he keeps the family savings habit.

steps.text: Test ten closed manufacturer returns in paid two-week trial if firm agrees
Take vendor lesson on paid firm time if trial reduces errors
Save two hundred monthly from current wages
Teach junior how factory stock ledgers link to tax returns if paid time granted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full AGI in 2028 makes the tax desk a different business. The partners need to tell clients and staff what human work they will still pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost all my work is thinking work, so 2028 is my danger date, not the robot date around 2031. I could lose a high salary if factories buy cheap AI returns, although ten months saved and many nearby firms give me choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add three hundred monthly to our reserve now and postpone buying the larger flat we discussed. In the first year after 2028, if Harborline cuts my paid hours, I'd apply for posted salaried factory finance roles and accept a paid temporary stock-audit contract only while searching for a stable wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our household income, even though we have a cushion. A year without my wage would change whether Anika and I can plan a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anika about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Anika that we can stay where we are until a salary offer is signed. We can make one small home work longer than we can make a missing wage appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start your own tax practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before finding clients who will pay a fee after AGI arrives. I would not use our family reserve to buy a business on hope alone.

say: I would ask Harborline to explain **human fees** to clients and staff.
I would say **2028 AGI** reaches the tax desk before robots.
think: My **high salary** could go if factories buy cheap AI returns.
Our **child plans** depend on a stable wage, despite ten months saved.
do: Save **three hundred more monthly** from my current salary.
Delay the **larger flat** until a signed salary offer.
Seek **posted salaried factory finance** or paid temporary stock-audit work if hours fall after 2028.
feel: He feels **anxious** about wage loss and delayed family plans.
S2.quote: We can make one small home work longer than we can make a missing wage appear.
fieldNote: He ties family plans to a **signed salary offer** and refuses to risk his reserve on a speculative practice.
His desk loses time in **2028**, while later robots are irrelevant to immediate tax work.

steps.text: Add three hundred monthly to family emergency reserve
Delay larger flat until signed salary offer
Apply for posted salaried factory finance roles if hours fall after 2028
Take paid temporary stock-audit contract while seeking stable wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm five years is enough to find a service factory owners will pay for and train staff to deliver it. I would want a price and a paid-hours budget, not just a new name for free advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I will still need a long career, and AGI can do the calculations behind our returns in 2031. But five years gives me a chance to build factory relationships and save a full year of bills before fees change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners next spring to let me pilot paid quarterly stock reviews with three existing manufacturer clients, with fees going to Harborline and the staff paid. In the first year after 2031, if two of the three renew at fees covering my hours, I'd stay on that salaried work; if not, I'd apply for advertised paid finance roles at manufacturers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, though a failed pilot would still tell me something useful. I can move with a real offer rather than jump because of a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each factory owner should sign for a second quarter at a fee that covers the reviewer and travel. If only one renews, we should stop calling it a viable service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the child plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anika and I would wait until we have twelve months of bills saved and one full year of steady wages from the new work. We want a child, but we would not count a trial fee as a permanent salary.

say: I would price **quarterly stock reviews** with paid staff hours.
I would stop if fewer than **two clients** renew at covering fees.
think: At **32 in 2031**, I need a long paid career beyond routine returns.
Five years lets me test **factory demand** before changing jobs.
do: Pilot **three paid stock reviews** with partner approval next spring.
Continue **salaried stock reviews** after 2031 only if two of three renewals cover staff and travel costs.
Apply for **advertised factory finance** roles if the pilot fails.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, but can use five years to test demand.
S3.quote: We want a child, but we would not count a trial fee as a permanent salary.
fieldNote: The firm-owned pilot has a **two-client renewal rule** and an explicit paid-hours budget.
His child plan waits for **steady wages** and twelve months saved, not a successful first quarter.

steps.text: Pilot paid quarterly stock reviews for three clients with partners approval
Continue salaried stock reviews after 2031 if two of three renewals fund staff and travel
Apply for advertised salaried factory finance roles if pilot fails
Wait to plan a child until twelve months saved and one steady year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to learn which parts of the factory accounts owners still want a person to explain. Harborline should test that in paid work each year, not make a grand promise now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 when AGI reaches desk work in 2036, I still need many years of income. Ten years could let us clear the flat loan and build a larger family reserve, even though robots around 2039 may change factory clients later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay an extra four hundred a month off our flat loan while salary remains high and build the stock-review service only with the partners' approval and paid staff time. In the first year after 2036, if the service covers my salary, I'd keep it; if client fees fall short, I'd apply for posted paid finance jobs and move only after a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to plan, but not indifferent. A decade is long enough to test whether our service earns its keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count renewals and compare the fee with staff and travel costs. I would shut a service that survives only because the team works unpaid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with firms on the train line and factories within a short commute. Anika and I would move homes only after a written salary offer covers the flat loan and her dental-clinic wage.

say: I would test **paid stock advice** year by year through Harborline.
I would stop work that depends on **unpaid staff hours**.
think: My desk remains exposed in **2036**, while the robot date is later.
Ten years may clear our **flat loan** and strengthen family savings.
do: Pay **four hundred extra monthly** against the flat loan while salary holds.
Track **paid stock-review renewals** with partner approval each year.
Seek **posted finance jobs** after 2036 cuts; move only with written pay covering the loan and my wife's wage.
feel: He feels **calm enough** to plan, while watching the service fee.
S4.quote: I would shut a service that survives only because the team works unpaid hours.
fieldNote: He uses strong earnings to **reduce debt** and refuses a service carried by unpaid hours.
A household move requires a **written offer** covering both the flat loan and Anika’s clinic income.

steps.text: Pay four hundred extra monthly against flat loan while salary holds
Track paid stock-review renewals with partners approval each year
Take posted paid finance job after 2036 fee shortfall only with written offer
Move home only if written salary covers flat loan and wife's clinic wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could cut my salary before we have made a firm plan for a child. A clear price for human review, a signed job offer if I must move and time to keep saving would help. An unsold accounting service cannot pay our family bills, however small our flat is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the factory owner what makes them call a human accountant after a machine has prepared the return. If no owner will pay for the answer, I need to hear that early.

headlineQuote: An unsold accounting service cannot pay our family bills, however small our flat is.
portrait: Yusuf, **27**, leads manufacturer returns at Harborline Accounts with a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
He earns **high pay**, has ten months saved and can reach many accounting firms by train.
He uses AI **occasionally after testing**, while Anika’s dental-clinic wage and their child plans shape his decisions.
He fears **2028 salary loss** most, then tests paid factory services and protects savings before family commitments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his high salary before he and Anika settle their child plans.
whatWouldHelp: A **human-review price**, time to save and a signed job offer before moving would help.
